(1) arsenic exposure causes a concentration‐dependent increase in gene expression in human primary lung cells, (2) the response is similar to that observed in primary uroephithelial cells, and (3) the response is unlikely to occur below 0.01 µg/ml (0.1 µm) in either cell type.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results of this study, in conjunction with the results of the previous study with human uroepithelium cells, provide evidence that the biological responses to arsenicals in human primary cells are unlikely to occur under study conditions at concentrations below 100 nM.

the results from this study and the previous study with uroepithelia cells are consistent and indicate that there is no evidence of a biologically relevant response at concentrations below 10 µM, and that there is a concentration‐related response above 10 µM.

the results of this study do not provide any evidence that arsenic exposure is associated with increased risk of lung cancer, and that the results are not consistent with the hypothesis that arsenic exposure increases lung cancer risk.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the human primary cell studies are consistent with the epidemiological studies in that there are effects at higher concentrations of exposure, and that there is no evidence of effects at low concentrations.
the data on human primary cells supports a conclusion that biological effects of arsenic are unlikely to occur under study conditions at arsenic concentrations below 0,1 µM.

the results indicate the need for a more careful evaluation of in vitro assays for their ability to predict the potential for in vivo effects, especially when extrapolating from in vitro to in vivo effects in humans.

we can identify a set of genes that respond similarly in two different cell types, and that these responses are consistent across individuals.
